prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
In the last days of August 1854, cholera arrived in Soho, a crowded and poor district of London, and in the space of about ten days killed roughly five hundred people living within a few streets of one another. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhoea and vomiting, and in those years it could drain a healthy adult of so much fluid that they died within a day or two. Nobody in London knew what caused it. The accepted view among doctors and officials was that it travelled in "miasma," a poisonous vapour rising from rotting rubbish, sewage and damp ground, and that the sensible response was to clean up bad smells and keep away from foul air.

John Snow, a physician who lived a short walk from the affected streets, did not accept this. He was best known for his work in anaesthesia, having given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth, and he had spent years thinking about cholera. His reasoning was that the illness struck the gut first, that people who nursed the sick often fell ill while people breathing the same air nearby did not, and that the disease must therefore be swallowed rather than inhaled, most likely in water contaminated with the waste of earlier victims. He had published this idea in 1849 to little effect, and he had also noticed during that earlier epidemic how differently cholera behaved in parts of south London depending on which water company supplied the houses. When the Soho outbreak began, he went door to door instead of arguing the point again.

He asked families where the dead had lived and what they had drunk, and he marked each death on a street map, with a bar drawn at the address for every victim. The bars gathered thickly around the public pump in Broad Street, where residents drew water for drinking and cooking, and they thinned as the distance from the pump increased. Snow also noticed that the pattern bent in a way that a cloud of bad air could hardly explain, because some people who lived closer to another pump were nevertheless dying, and when he asked, he learned that they preferred the Broad Street water and walked there to fetch it. He took samples of the water and examined them, but under the microscope he found nothing conclusive, and he knew that this would not persuade anyone on its own.

What persuaded him, and what remains persuasive, were the cases that did not fit. A workhouse on nearby Poland Street housed more than five hundred people, almost surrounded by deaths, yet only a handful of its inmates died, and Snow found that the workhouse had its own well and never touched the Broad Street pump. The brewery on the same street lost none of its workers, who were given malt liquor to drink and, in any case, had a well of their own on the premises. Most striking of all was a widow living in Hampstead, far from the epidemic, who died along with her niece after a cart brought bottles of water from the Broad Street pump because she had grown fond of its taste; her son had once run a factory near the pump, and she had formed the habit years before.

On the evening of 7 September, Snow took his evidence to the board of guardians of the local parish of St James, the men then responsible for the neighbourhood, and urged them to remove the handle from the pump so that nobody could draw from it. They agreed, whether because he convinced them or because they had no better idea, and the handle came off the next day. The legend that the epidemic ended at that moment is a little too tidy, since deaths had already been falling for several days as many residents fled and the sick died off, and Snow said so himself. Even so, the removal of the handle has stayed in memory as the moment when an idea was acted on.

The part of the story that tends to be forgotten is how much remained unsettled. Snow had shown that the pump was the centre of the outbreak but not why it had become dangerous, and here he was helped by Henry Whitehead, a young curate who knew the families in the parish and who had at first set out to prove Snow wrong. Whitehead discovered that a baby girl at number 40 Broad Street had died of what looked like cholera shortly before the outbreak, that her mother had washed the child's soiled nappies and tipped the water into a cesspool beside the house, and that the cesspool lay only a few feet from the well. When the well was dug up some time later, the brick lining was found to be cracked, which would have let filthy seepage run straight into the supply.

Even with this, the official inquiry into the outbreak concluded that the water was not to blame, and Snow died in 1858 still without general agreement. It took the careful identification of the cholera bacterium by Robert Koch in the 1880s, and the long, expensive work of building proper sewers and clean water supplies across London, before his view became common knowledge. The method he used, which was to map where illness fell, ask what the sick had in common, and then look hardest at the people who should have been ill and were not, became one of the foundations of modern epidemiology.
